newsitem.title: FRANCE: EP wants tougher measures to clean up drinking water.
newsitem.headline: EP wants tougher measures to clean up drinking water.

text.p: The European Parliament demanded on Thursday stricter measures to clean up Europe's drinking water, namely by strictly limiting the permitted lead and pesticides content.
The European Commission has proposed to tighten up a 1980 EU directive on the quality of drinking water but the Parliament said the proposal, while welcome, did not go far enough.

In its proposal -- COM(94)612 -- the Commission follows the line adopted by the World Health Organisation in recommending an 80 percent cut in the maximum allowed lead content from 50 miligrammes per litre to 25mg/l within five years, and to 10mg/l after 15.
But Parliament adopted a report by environment committee chairman Ken Collins which says the member states should have to meet the 10mg/l target after only 10 years.

Setting a 10mg/l maximum -- an 80 percent cut -- will entail replacing miles and miles of old lead pipes with plastic ones, particularly in Belgium, Britain, France, Spain, Portugal and Italy and Ireland.
Countries could comply with the 25mg/l limit -- a 50 percent drop -- by treating water chemically.

Parliament also rejected the Commission's proposal on pesticides, that is a retention of the existing limit of 0.1 microgrammes of pesticide per litre for individual pesticides but scraps the 0.5 microgrammes per litre cumulative total.
Euro-MPs insisted the cumulative total should be maintained.

Collins' report insists the EU must not relax its pressure on member states to clean up water supplies, especially in the light of their dismal record of compliance with the existing directive, which has been in force for 16 years.
As well as lead and pesticides, it sets tougher limits on nitrates, heavy metals and radioactive particles.
The amendments on lead, which Parliament demanded at this first reading of the proposal, were not supported by French Christian Democrat Euro-MPs.
Replacing lead pipes throughout the EU would cost between 35 and 50 billion Ecus, Euro-MP Francoise Grossetete told reporters after the vote.

Grossetete would have preferred to force member states to meet the 25mg/l limit within five years, during which time toxicological studies should be carried out into the effect of lead and plastic piping on human health.
Only then should the EU consider imposing more stringent measures, she said.
In the meantime, pregnant women and babies of bottle-feeding age should only drink bottled water, the French Euro-MP said.
The drinking water proposal is one of two analyses of water policy which the Parliament approved on Thursday under the cooperation procedure.
The other concerns a Commission proposal to clean up Europe's bathing waters -- COM(94)36.
The two proposals are "daughter directives" to a planned framework directive on the EU's overall water policy which the Parliament approved in October.
